entries.subject: Remove DUPOK and NOPROF flags from asm functions.
entries.message:
Remove DUPOK and NOPROF flags from asm functions.

runtime/textflag.h defines:
NOPROF  1
DUPOK   2
NOSPLIT 4

The DUPOK bit was why the bug in
https://github.com/klauspost/compress/commit/6ea72a38a8cdbe25966059c547d425e580c624a7
wasn't picked up earlier.

The existing 7 is presumably a copy/paste of some standard library asm
code. It's a legacy idiom that really should be 5 or 4. See
https://groups.google.com/d/msg/golang-nuts/uJTYuruvnZM/6j4KXgkdcf0J for
some history.

Asm code in the standard library uses NOSPLIT instead of 4 these days.

WithEncoderPadding will add padding to all output so the size will be a multiple of n.

The contents will be a skippable frame, so it will be invisible by the decoder.

If `EncodeAll` is used with data already in the destination, the total size will be multiple of this.

a request for several ranges (as written by http.ServeContent) has no
Content-Range header, so it was compressed: the client got a 206 with
"Content-Encoding: gzip" and Accept-Ranges removed, although the ranges in its
parts refer to the uncompressed representation.

Treat the 206 status like the Content-Range header in Write, Flush and Close.

* gzhttp: read Accept-Encoding across field lines

A client may split one Accept-Encoding list over several field lines, which
means the same as the joined comma list (RFC 9110, section 5.3). selectEncoding
and acceptsGzip used Header.Get, which only returns the first line, so
"Accept-Encoding: deflate" followed by "Accept-Encoding: gzip" was answered
without compression, and a later q-value such as "zstd;q=0" was ignored.

Join the field lines before parsing, the same way the request Content-Encoding
is already read, and share the helper between the two.

* gzhttp: remove the unused acceptsGzip

entries.subject: zstd: fix arm64 asm locals overwriting the saved link register (#1176)
entries.message:
zstd: fix arm64 asm locals overwriting the saved link register (#1176)

The generated arm64 decoder assembly places every function local 8 bytes
too low, so local 0 lands on the saved link register.

x86 and arm64 put the return address in different places. On x86, CALL
pushes it before the callee runs, so it sits above the frame and local 0
is at SP+0. On arm64, BL leaves it in the link register and the callee
spills it to the BOTTOM of its own frame, so 0(RSP) is the saved LR and
locals start at 8(RSP). The avo arm64 lowering renamed the pseudo stack
pointer to RSP and passed the displacement through unchanged, inheriting
x86's layout.

Verified by disassembling probe functions at two frame sizes: for both
TEXT $8 and TEXT $64 the assembler places pseudo-SP local 0 at 8(RSP),
while the prologue's MOVD.W R30, -N(RSP) puts the saved LR at 0(RSP).
The 8-byte offset does not depend on frame size.

Affected: sequenceDecs_decode_arm64, sequenceDecs_decode_56_arm64,
sequenceDecs_decodeSync_arm64 and sequenceDecs_decodeSync_safe_arm64,
all present since v1.19.0.

Scope: this does NOT corrupt decoded data and cannot produce wrong
output. Every local shifts by the same 8 bytes, so loads and stores
agree and the arithmetic is self-consistent; that is why the test suite
and fuzzing never caught it. These are leaf functions, so the link
register is still live in R30 and RET works. What breaks is the unwind
path only: GC stack scanning, panics and profiling read the return
address from 0(RSP) and find decoder state there.

The fix shifts pseudo-SP displacements by 8 in the lowering, so the
regenerated assembly is a mechanical +8 on every local access and
nothing else. zstd tests pass on arm64 (Neoverse N1).

entries.subject: maint(all): drop legacy build tags and old-Go workarounds (#1242)
entries.message:
maint(all): drop legacy build tags and old-Go workarounds (#1242)

* all: drop the appengine build tag and legacy +build lines

The appengine tag selected pure-Go code for the classic App Engine
runtime, which no longer exists; noasm and nounsafe cover that need.
Go has read //go:build since 1.17, so the // +build lines are dead too.

The zstd and s2 generators also added !noasm twice. Their constraints
now match huff0's single ConstraintExpr, and s2 only adds the
(amd64 || arm64) term to the run that writes the shared stubs, so the
arm64 file no longer reads arm64 && ((amd64 || arm64) && ...).

The compiled file set (go list GoFiles, SFiles, TestGoFiles) is
identical to before for amd64, arm64, 386, riscv64 and ppc64le with no
tags, noasm, nounsafe, noasm,nounsafe and purego. Regenerated assembly
differs only in its header.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* all: drop build constraints every supported Go version satisfies

go.mod requires Go 1.25, so the go1.16, go1.18 and go1.24 constraints
always hold. zstd/simple_go124.go and its test only existed for the
constraint and become simple.go and simple_test.go.

zip carried copies of fs.FormatDirEntry and fs.FormatFileInfo until Go

archive/zip does. The gzhttp test builds its request with
httptest.NewRequest, as its Go 1.6-era TODO asked, and a comment about
pre-1.20 builds goes.

TestEncodeTo sat in its own file only because of the go1.24 tag; it

entries.subject: huff0: align the decode inner loops to 64 bytes (#1236)
entries.message:
huff0: align the decode inner loops to 64 bytes (#1236)

* huff0: move the asm generator to the current avo arm64 fork

The honeycombio/avo fork adds a PCALIGN pseudo-instruction that the arm64
lowering passes through. The regenerated assembly is byte-identical. The
newer avo requires newer golang.org/x modules, which require go 1.25.0.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* huff0: align the decode inner loops to 64 bytes

Place PCALIGN $64 before the 4X and 1X inner loops, which also raises
each function's alignment to 64. Without it the loop heads land wherever
the linker places the function, and the same code measured about ±2%
apart between builds that differed only in what came before it. The
padding runs once per outer iteration.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* huff0: move the asm generator to avo with the PCALIGN label check

The honeycombio/avo fork now rejects a label placed directly on a
PCALIGN, which the amd64 assembler mishandles (golang/go#74648,
golang/go#81792). The regenerated assembly is byte-identical.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

zstd: Add ResetWithOptions to encoder/decoder (#1122)

## New API Methods

```
  func (*Encoder) ResetWithOptions(w io.Writer, opts ...EOption) error
  func (*Decoder) ResetWithOptions(r io.Reader, opts ...DOption) error

```

New Options

  // Encoder - clears dictionary
  `WithEncoderDictDelete() EOption`

  // Decoder - removes dicts by ID; no args clears all
  `WithDecoderDictDelete(ids ...uint32) DOption`

Option Reset Compatibility

  Can be changed with ResetWithOptions:
  - Encoder: WithEncoderCRC, WithEncoderPadding, WithZeroFrames, WithAllLitEntropyCompression, WithNoEntropyCompression, WithSingleSegment, WithEncoderDict, WithEncoderDictRaw, WithEncoderDictDelete
  - Decoder: WithDecoderMaxMemory, WithDecoderMaxWindow, WithDecoderDicts, WithDecoderDictRaw, WithDecoderDictDelete, WithDecodeAllCapLimit, IgnoreChecksum

  Cannot be changed with ResetWithOptions:
  - Encoder: WithEncoderConcurrency, WithWindowSize, WithEncoderLevel, WithLowerEncoderMem
  - Decoder: WithDecoderLowmem, WithDecoderConcurrency, WithDecodeBuffersBelow

entries.subject: s2: Add AsyncFlush method: Complete the block without flushing (#927)
entries.message:
s2: Add AsyncFlush method: Complete the block without flushing (#927)

* s2: Add AsyncFlush method: Complete the block without flushing

My use case is to transfer a large compressed S2 stream with a few
changes very often. To get a small diff I want to end blocks at
application decided points rather than at byte offsets. This allows me
to remove the first byte without every single block changing.

Flush() works for this, but it limits concurrency because it waits for
the last block to be compressed rather than allowing that
asynchronously.

So I'd like to propose AsyncFlush, which flushes the buffer to a block,
but doesn't flush the block to the io.Writer.

There were actually a few places in the s2 code that also wanted to end
the block, but didn't necessary want to flush to the writer.

entries.subject: gzhttp: only decompress a request when gzip is the outermost coding (#1223)
entries.message:
gzhttp: only decompress a request when gzip is the outermost coding (#1223)

* gzhttp: only decompress a request when gzip is the outermost coding

contentGzip used parseEncodingGzip, which scans a comma list for gzip in any
position with q-values. That is an Accept-Encoding parser: Accept-Encoding is
an unordered preference set, so acceptsGzip is right to use it. Content-Encoding
lists codings in the order they were applied, so only the last one is the
outermost coding a decoder may remove.

Two consequences for a handler wrapped with AllowCompressedRequests(true):

  Content-Encoding: gzip, deflate   the body is deflate on the outside, but it
                                    was fed to a gzip reader and the handler
                                    got "gzip: invalid header"
  Content-Encoding: br, gzip        gunzipping is correct, but deleting the
                                    whole header hid that br is still applied

Decide on the last coding and strip only that one, leaving the rest in place.
The single "Content-Encoding: gzip" case is unchanged.

* gzhttp: read Content-Encoding across field lines

A sender may split one Content-Encoding list over several field lines, which
means the same as the joined comma list. Header.Get returns only the first of
them, so "Content-Encoding: gzip" followed by "Content-Encoding: deflate" was
read as gzip alone and the body was fed to a gzip reader although deflate is
the outermost coding. The reverse pair was left undecoded for the same reason.

Join the field lines before deciding and before rewriting.

The three-coding test case declared br and deflate but the fixture applied
neither, so it asserted nothing about them. Use three gzip layers instead,
which the fixture can really apply, and assert that exactly one is removed.

* gzhttp: make the content-encoding cases round trip

Move the cases into compress_test.go instead of a new file, and encode each
request body with exactly the codings it declares so the handler can decode
whatever is left and compare against testBody. A pass now means the payload
survived compression and decompression byte for byte, rather than that one
header string matched.

No test in the package read r.Body before this, so the request-decompression
path was only covered by a response-length check.

* gzhttp: use strings.SplitSeq in the content-encoding test

go fix flags strings.Split here; the CI fix gate runs go fix -diff over the
whole module.

entries.subject: zstd: stream a small buffer when its in-memory decode exceeds the size limit (#1207)
entries.message:
zstd: stream a small buffer when its in-memory decode exceeds the size limit (#1207)

Decoder.Reset decodes a source with Bytes and Len shorter than
WithDecodeBuffersBelow in one go through DecodeAll, where
WithDecoderMaxMemory caps the total decoded size. A Reader is documented
with the streaming contract, where the option caps the window instead,
so the same Reader followed one rule or the other depending on input
length: a 1740-byte frame with no content size that expands past a
20 MiB limit failed over a bytes.Buffer and decoded over any other
io.Reader.

When the shortcut's DecodeAll reports ErrDecoderSizeExceeded, fall
through to the normal streaming decode of the same reader, whose bytes
the shortcut has not consumed. Memory stays bounded as documented: the
in-memory attempt stops at the cap, its buffer is dropped, and streaming
holds a window.

Found by a differential fuzz harness while fuzzing #1204; the stock
fuzzers share the threshold on both sides and cannot see it.

Fixes #1206

entries.subject: s2: fix LZ4 block conversion writing past dst (#1244)
entries.message:
s2: fix LZ4 block conversion writing past dst (#1244)

* s2: stop LZ4 block conversion from writing past dst

The literal bound in the S2-output converters ignored the 1-5 byte
literal header, leaving too little room for a following copy with a
5-byte repeat (up to 8 bytes). The assembly wrote a few bytes past
cap(dst) before returning ErrDstTooSmall; the pure-Go path panicked.
Matches over ~16.8 MB chained 5-byte repeat chunks with no check, so the
overrun grew with the match length.

Tighten the existing literal bound so a copy always fits, and check the
limit only before each extra repeat chunk. The Snappy-output converters
already checked every chunk.

Add an unexported noAsm field so tests reach the pure-Go path without
build tags.

* s2: fuzz LZ4 conversion with under- and oversized dst

FuzzLZ4Block gave the converter 2*len(data)+4096 bytes, which S2 output
never comes close to, and asm writes past cap(dst) are invisible without
a guard. Convert again with every variant into need +/- a deterministic
amount up to len(data), with 16 guard bytes after cap, and check the
guard and that the result agrees with the large-dst run.

On the unfixed code this found an overrun within minutes; the input is
added to the seed corpus.

* s2: fuzz LZ4 assembly only when available

FuzzLZ4Block covers the assembly and pure-Go converters in one run, so
add the assembly variants only when hasAsm is set, and run the fuzzer in
CI without the noasm,nounsafe pass, on both amd64 and arm64.
